title: Fannin County Folk and Fact, Page 60 — Education / Fannin County Schools 1838-1900
text:
EDUCATION

While there was no organized system of education in Texas when the first settlers came to Fannin County, all the families knew the value of education and worked to provide some sort of academic training for their children. The first schools were neighborhood schools, established by churches or people in the communities and parents usually paid a great deal of the credit must go to local men who located school, sometimes several families joined together to hire a teacher to educate their children. Many times the teacher boarded with the families and received their pay in farm produce.

In many villages school buildings were simple log cabins usually with split-log seats, slab tables and dirt floors. Even the larger and better schools had poor equipment and the length of school days and school terms varied depending on weather, the threat of Indian attack, or the planting and harvesting when the children were needed at home.

A typical school day was spent learning the bedrock three R's — reading, 'riting, 'rithmetic — with an occasional subject as history, geography, and such subjects as art. Great importance was placed on repetition and memory work. Students recited their lessons aloud in unison. The rod was a widely accepted educational practice by educational axiom practiced by every teacher of the day, and the importance placed by every child switch was very much a part of the normal day as were the grueling spelling bees and debates during school hours.

"It is to their undying credit," the early historian continued, "that the Indians gathered no scalps, at least while Savoy College students were around and at least while Savoy College graduates went out into the world and became doctors, lawyers, judges, preachers, teachers and businessmen. Several even became missionaries and taught in the Orient."

A state school system was tried in 1876 when counties were expected to provide facilities and assume local control and even to sell them. With localized control of schools

the community system came into existence and Texas at last provided a free public school system. No sooner had the system been put into effect than it was found to be faulty. By 1882 the average school term for most East Texas counties was 3-8 months and few school districts had been able to comply. Despite these shortcomings in 1882 every county in Texas used this community school system for the public schools.

It was not until the reconstruction era that the community school of Texas lost its status as being the best method of reaching children and getting money for taxes ... may be used for ... buying school sites, buying, constructing and equipping school buildings, controls and clearly defined legislation which supported the laws operating only for rapid development of the public school system in Texas.

The strong determination and unselfish dedication of many Fannin County residents provided the children of the area with a community school system during Texas' early growing period. Without the advantages of organized public or private education, the people of Fannin County could not have progressed as did the rest of the county. Few counties could boast of the same number of educators and the same diversity of instruction as was offered or the quality of education as could Fannin County.

FANNIN COUNTY SCHOOLS 1838-1900

The first school in Fannin County was in a stable at Warpen, one of the first settlements in the county near Red River. The teacher, whose name is not known, looked around for a school and obtained permission from the owner of the stable to use it. The stable became a school building by moving the horses and cattle to the open air. The students sat on wooden legs in holes drilled in the rough side of the logs to form the seats. The seats had no backs, but pupils managed to stay on them. The teacher had twenty pupils from nine to fifteen with ten pupils. There is no record of how long it continued or if anyone ever learned anything of value from that school. The information about the first school was taken from a reminiscent article that appeared in the Paris, Texas, papers of the 1880s and 1890s.

Education for children and youth was carried on in numerous small schools from 1838 to 1876, generally with one teacher, until the late 1860's when several in different parts of the county were growing and were established.

A state school system was tried in 1876 when counties were expected to provide facilities and assume local control and even to sell them. With localized control of schools, communities in Fannin County became centers for private accommodation for the more advanced subjects such as Latin, Greek, philosophy and geography were taught compulsory were strictly enforced. Carlton College in Bonham and the Savoy Male College were the best of the district's two leading colleges in the area.

FANNIN COUNTY SCHOOLS

The first school in Fannin was in a stable at Warpen, one of the first settlements in the county near Red River. Carlton College in Bonham, established in 1867 in Bonham by Charles Carlton. During its operation, Carlton and one or two of his daughters made up the complete faculty with civic minded faculty with civic minded teachers at different times from year to year. As president of the college and for Pastor of the First Methodist Church, Carlton taught Latin, Biblical Literature, Mathematics, Moral Philosophy, Latin, Biblical Literature, Mathematics, Moral Philosophy, and also taught drawing and painting. His daughter, Sallie Joe, taught music and a variety of other subjects.

The influence of this college was profound. The girls were to wear a uniform of simple navy blue material and at Commencement they were to wear white muslin dresses. The influence of this college which operated until about 1891 educated and influenced and talented women in the county for two generations.
